new: The shape of the chapter is simple.
It opens with one concrete refund decision, a predicate that answers it for free, and a walkthrough you can run.
It then sets out the model-backed routes, which have not yet been run, against the one value the application actually reads.
It sets out the four words the rest of the book will keep apart, and closes with the one question it cannot yet answer.
The errors look policy-shaped: they fall where the rule's numeric conditions are met but its intent is not covered.
Whether a model would share that shape is not yet known; Chapter 7 and the arms below are where that is tested.
dropped: The prompt is identical for both model-backed paths, which matters: any difference between them is attributable to the decoding constraint, not to a differently worded request.
**DOCUMENTED.** Two details from their §1 and §5 earn their place here.

The obvious implementation — score the whole vocabulary each step and zero out the inadmissible tokens — costs O(N) per token with N the vocabulary size, which they note is often 10^4 or larger; the indexed version is O(1) on average.
And the index is not free: even naively built for an augmented Python grammar, they report it at "around 50 MB".
Constraint is a memory cost before it is a compute win.
The guarantee is worth stating precisely, because it is routinely overclaimed.

The measurements in this chapter are the evidence that conflating them is expensive.
Whether a decision deserves to be a programming construct is [Chapter 16](/books/jev/16-chapter/).
Whether a decision model is a distinct category of model is [Chapter 2](/books/jev/02-chapter/).

That is the whole claim so far: generation and decision are not the same act; the programming-construct question is [Chapter 16](/books/jev/16-chapter/), and the model-category question is [Chapter 2](/books/jev/02-chapter/). ## What we measured, and what we did not The experiment was pre-registered *before* any run.

What Chapter 1 leaves standing is an open question handed to Chapter 2, a vendor contract recorded as a third-party claim rather than a specification to be trusted, and a summary held to one line until the primary sources are read.
